questions.prompt: What is the core move in the alliance strategy?
choices: Find genuine overlap so a stronger actor benefits from advancing you
Rely on admiration from powerful people
Hide your own interests completely from potential sponsors

explanation.gentle: The chapter defines alliance as real interest alignment rather than generalized support.
explanation.direct: Start with the mechanism: a stronger actor moves hardest when your progress also serves that actor's own aims.
explanation.competitive: The move is to hook your rise into someone else's incentive engine.

questions.prompt: Why does genuine overlap usually matter more than goodwill in this chapter?
choices: Because goodwill automatically creates permanent loyalty
Because real incentive match usually survives pressure better than sentiment
Because stronger actors never care about outcomes

explanation.gentle: Goodwill can help early, but the chapter says durable support usually depends on real self-interest.
explanation.direct: Keep the durability test clear: incentives tend to hold longer than warm language once cost rises.
explanation.competitive: Sentiment leaks fast when pressure shows up. Interest usually leaks slower.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reversal about alliance?
choices: Any sponsor relationship becomes safer over time
Borrowed leverage is identical to loyalty
Pseudo-alignment can create early motion and still collapse once incentives are tested

explanation.gentle: The warning is that staged overlap may look strong before real costs expose the weakness.
explanation.direct: Notice the reversal: support can appear solid early and still thin out fast if the incentive match was never real.
explanation.competitive: Fake alignment often runs until the bill arrives.

questions.prompt: Imogen wants stronger executive backing. What best fits the chapter?
choices: Frame the project around the executive's concrete objective that the project would improve
Stress that supporting the team would look generous to others
Avoid discussing the executive's incentives so the pitch sounds less transactional

explanation.gentle: Imogen succeeds once she connects the project to a goal the stronger actor already cares about.
explanation.direct: Focus on the overlap: backing gets stronger when the sponsor's own scoreboard improves through the project.
explanation.competitive: Sell the win that helps them win too.

questions.prompt: Rourke says alliance is not just networking charm. What is he emphasizing?
choices: That stronger actors should always be emotionally attached first
That durable alliance depends on real incentive overlap rather than atmosphere alone
That all alliances should stay hidden from public view

explanation.gentle: Rourke keeps bringing the room back to whether the other side really benefits from your progress.
explanation.direct: Distinguish mood from structure: charm may start contact, but overlap is what carries the arrangement.
explanation.competitive: Pleasant chemistry is not the same thing as locked incentives.

questions.prompt: Brisa wants an enterprise advocate who will keep pushing after the first excitement fades. Which move best fits the chapter?
choices: Ask for support based only on the partnership's inspiring story
Make the advocate's internal win materially stronger if the partnership succeeds
Avoid asking what the advocate personally needs from the arrangement

explanation.gentle: The chapter favors real internal benefit over symbolic enthusiasm.
explanation.direct: Test for durability: the advocate should keep gaining something concrete after the easy phase ends.
explanation.competitive: Give the ally internal upside or expect the pull to fade.

questions.prompt: Tavish is getting doors opened by one influential sponsor. When does the chapter say caution is warranted?
choices: Only when the sponsor offers too much useful help
When he starts treating one sponsor's support as if it were permanent loyalty
Only when no incentives overlap at all

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that even real support stays conditional on continuing overlap.
explanation.direct: Separate usefulness from permanence: borrowed leverage is strongest when it is managed as contingent.
explanation.competitive: The danger starts when rented force gets mistaken for owned force.

questions.prompt: A coalition uses unified language, but members benefit differently and carry different risks. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: The coalition may be speaking as one while resting on uneven or unstable overlap
The shared language proves the incentives are aligned enough
The incentive mismatch makes all cooperation impossible

explanation.gentle: Shared language can still hide a fragile structure underneath.
explanation.direct: Check the incentive map directly: rhetoric cannot substitute for overlap analysis.
explanation.competitive: A banner is not an alignment audit.

questions.prompt: Which judgment best captures the chapter's ethical and strategic limit?
choices: Alliance is strongest when the weaker party hides costs from the stronger one
Alliance works only when affection is fully mutual
The strategy stays sound only when the overlap is honest enough that the stronger party is not being carried by a false theory of benefit

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether the support would still make sense after an honest accounting of benefit and cost.
explanation.direct: Judge the method by truthfulness: once the other side's benefit is staged rather than real, both ethics and durability weaken.
explanation.competitive: If the alliance needs a lie to stay alive, collapse is already in the structure.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 27 differ from the one-upmanship logic that follows in Chapter 28?
choices: Chapter 27 and Chapter 28 both rely on the same mechanism of moral framing
Chapter 27 denies targets while Chapter 28 builds sponsorship
Chapter 27 gains force through genuine overlap, while Chapter 28 profits from letting rivals overextend themselves

explanation.gentle: The bridge moves from allied incentive to rival self-damage.
explanation.direct: Bridge the next step cleanly: this chapter builds through mutual advantage, while the next one exploits overreach.
explanation.competitive: Here you recruit stronger motion. Next chapter you let ego and excess do the damage for you.
